question: A 63-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his wife because she is concerned he is having another stroke. The patient says he woke up with right-sided facial weakness and drooping. Past medical history is significant for a recent case of shingles treated with acyclovir, and a stroke, diagnosed 10 years ago, from which he recovered with no residual functional deficits. On physical examination, there is weakness and drooping of the entire right side of the face. Sensation is intact. The remainder of the physical examination is unremarkable. Which of the following additional findings would also most likely be seen in this patient?

options.opc: Complete loss of taste to the tongue

analysis: The patient's symptoms are consistent with Bell's palsy, which is a peripheral facial nerve (cranial nerve VII) palsy. This condition typically results in weakness of the entire side of the face, including the forehead, because the facial nerve innervates all the muscles of facial expression. In Bell's palsy, additional symptoms can include decreased salivation, partial hearing loss (due to hyperacusis from stapedius muscle paralysis), and loss of taste to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. However, complete loss of taste is unlikely as it would require additional nerve involvement. Expressive aphasia is related to central nervous system issues, such as a stroke affecting Broca's area, and is not associated with Bell's palsy. A wrinkled forehead would indicate sparing of the forehead muscles, which is not typical in Bell's palsy. Therefore, partial hearing loss is a plausible additional finding due to the involvement of the facial nerve.
